questions.prompt: Put these six stages of working a support ticket, per Lesson 1, in the order they occur.
items: Intake — the ticket is logged: who reported it, what they saw, when, and on which record
Triage — severity and priority are assigned
Reproduce and scope — confirm the problem is real and work out how far it extends
Investigate — trace the symptom back through the setup, data, and process to find the actual cause
Resolve — apply the fix and verify it
Document and close — record what happened, why, and what you did
questions.explain: Every ticket in this course moves through the same six stages in this order: intake, triage, reproduce and scope, investigate, resolve, document and close. Chapters 2 through 6 live almost entirely in Investigate and Resolve, worked through real ticket scenarios.

questions.prompt: Match each Lesson 1 key term to what it actually means.
right: How urgent a ticket is, based on impact and how many people are blocked
The actual condition in the setup or data that produced the symptom, not the symptom itself
Confirm the issue is real by triggering it yourself or walking through the same steps the user took
How far the problem extends — one record, one user, one business unit, or everyone
questions.explain: Reproduce means confirming the issue is real yourself. Scope means working out how far it extends. Root cause is the actual condition behind the symptom, not the symptom itself. Severity is about urgency and impact — and, per the lesson, it tells you nothing about why something is actually broken.

questions.prompt: One user reports they can't see a journal that everyone else on the team can see fine. Per Lesson 2's diagnostic method, what does this specific pattern point to first?
options: Security or a role assignment, not a data problem
A disabled account combination affecting the journal
The accounting period being closed
A failed Journal Import run
questions.explain: Lesson 2's second diagnostic question is exactly this: if one person can't see something and everyone else can, that's almost always security or a role assignment, not a data problem. If nobody could see it, you'd look at the data and setup instead.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 6, which statement correctly describes the difference between 2-way, 3-way, and 4-way invoice matching?
options: 2-way matches PO price and quantity ordered; 3-way adds the quantity received; 4-way adds an inspection record
2-way matches price and quantity received; 3-way adds quantity ordered; 4-way adds an inspection record
2-way, 3-way, and 4-way all check the identical set of fields, differing only in approval routing
3-way matching checks price only; 2-way checks quantity only
4-way matching is required on every invoice regardless of how the purchase order line is configured
2-way matching always includes the possibility of a Qty Rec hold, the same as 3-way matching
questions.explain: 2-way matching checks the PO's price and quantity ordered. 3-way matching adds the receipt — quantity actually received. 4-way matching adds an inspection record on top of that. The matching level is configured on the PO line and determines which holds are even possible.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F is the tempting trap: it sounds like it's just adding detail, but it's actually backwards. A 2-way match never looks at receiving at all, so it can never produce a Qty Rec hold — only 3-way (and 4-way) matching, which actually checks the receipt, can.

questions.prompt: An invoice's price is $55 against a PO price of $50 — a 10% increase that exceeds a 5% tolerance — and the supplier's contract price genuinely did increase. Per Lesson 5, which fix correctly addresses this, rather than just clearing the symptom?
options: Update the purchase order to the new, confirmed price and resubmit Validation
Manually release the Price hold so the invoice can be paid immediately
Change the invoice price back to $50 to match the PO
Apply a payment term discount equal to the price difference
questions.explain: When the PO price is genuinely stale, the correct fix is updating the PO itself. Manually releasing the hold clears this one invoice but posts the difference to a variance account and leaves the PO wrong for every future shipment from that supplier.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the common Payables hold types from Lesson 5.
options: A Price hold means the invoiced price exceeds the PO price beyond tolerance
A Qty Ord hold means the quantity billed exceeds the quantity received beyond tolerance
A Tax Variance hold means the invoice's tax amount doesn't match what Oracle calculates from the configured tax rate
An Account hold means a distribution references an invalid or disabled account
Manually releasing a hold corrects the underlying variance that caused it
questions.explain: Price, Tax Variance, and Account holds are described exactly this way in Lesson 5's table. Qty Ord actually means the quantity billed exceeds the quantity ordered — exceeding quantity received is the Qty Rec hold, a different hold entirely. And manually releasing a hold clears it for that one invoice without fixing the underlying variance.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle Fusion Payables always runs the ________ duplicate invoice check automatically, comparing business unit, supplier, supplier site, and invoice number, with nothing to configure.
questions.explain: The standard duplicate invoice check always runs with no configuration needed. A separate, optional check (enabled through a lookup code) compares supplier, invoice type, amount, currency, and date instead, to catch invoices that arrived under a different invoice number.

questions.prompt: Match each Payables hold to what it actually means.
right: The invoice's tax amount doesn't match the amount Oracle calculates from the configured tax rate
The quantity billed exceeds the quantity received beyond tolerance
The invoiced price exceeds the purchase order price beyond the allowed tolerance
The quantity billed exceeds the quantity ordered beyond tolerance
questions.explain: Price compares invoiced price to PO price. Qty Ord compares quantity billed to quantity ordered. Qty Rec compares quantity billed to quantity actually received (only possible under 3-way or 4-way matching). Tax Variance compares the invoice's tax amount to what Oracle calculates from the configured rate.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a Payment Process Request, per Lesson 9, in the order they execute.
items: Select gathers eligible invoices into the batch
Build attempts to construct the actual payment documents
Format produces the output file sent to the bank
Confirm finalizes the payment
questions.explain: A PPR moves through Select, Build, Format, then Confirm. A failure can happen at any of these stages, and the error you see depends entirely on which one it is — a Build-stage validation failure looks nothing like a Format-stage file issue.

questions.prompt: A supplier's payment terms are correctly set to Net 45 at the supplier level, but invoices against one specific supplier site are defaulting to Net 15. Per Lesson 10, what does this most likely mean, and what's the correct fix?
options: The supplier site has its own Net 15 override, which takes precedence over the supplier-level value; correct the site-level terms
The supplier-level value is being ignored by Oracle entirely, so the supplier record itself needs to be rebuilt
This is expected behavior, and no site-level value ever overrides a supplier-level value
The invoices simply need to be re-validated for the supplier-level terms to apply automatically
questions.explain: When a site-level value is specified, it overrides the supplier-level value for invoices entered against that site — the site is more specific, and more specific wins. The fix is correcting the site-level terms, and any already-entered invoices still need correcting individually, since a setup fix only changes what defaults going forward.

questions.prompt: A controller finds the Receivables aging total is $6,500 lower than the AR control account balance in GL. Drilling into the GL journal detail for the account shows one manually entered journal for exactly $6,500 posted directly to the AR control account, with no corresponding Receivables transaction. What's the correct fix?
options: Reverse the direct GL journal and enter the equivalent adjustment as a proper Receivables transaction against the correct customer
Leave the GL journal in place, since the dollar amount already reconciles the two balances
Delete the Receivables aging report and regenerate it so it matches GL
Post an offsetting $6,500 journal directly to GL to zero out the difference
questions.explain: A direct journal posted straight to the AR control account bypasses the subledger entirely, so the subledger and GL disagree by that amount. The adjustment itself may be legitimate, but the fix is reversing the direct journal and entering the equivalent adjustment as a Receivables transaction, so it flows through the subledger and reconciles naturally going forward.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a receipt misapplied to the wrong invoice, per Lesson 12.
options: It creates two incorrect balances at once: the actually-paid invoice still shows open, and the wrongly-applied invoice shows paid when it wasn't
Unapplying and reapplying a receipt deletes the original, incorrect application from the record entirely
A misapplied receipt can have downstream effects, like an incorrect customer statement or an unwarranted dunning notice
A receipt can only ever be applied to exactly one invoice immediately, with no possibility of sitting unapplied
questions.explain: A misapplied receipt leaves the real invoice open and makes the wrong invoice look paid — two incorrect balances from one mistake. It can also cause downstream problems like a wrong statement or an unwarranted dunning letter, which is why Lesson 12 says to check further than just the two invoices. Unapplying and reapplying preserves history rather than deleting it, and a receipt can sit unapplied, "on account," before it's ever matched to an invoice.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: during AutoInvoice import, any transaction line that fails validation is diverted into the interface error table ________ instead of becoming a Receivables transaction.
questions.explain: RA_INTERFACE_ERRORS_ALL holds every line AutoInvoice couldn't import. A line rejected for missing setup shows only a count with no reason given; a line that goes into error shows the actual error detail — a distinction that changes how you investigate.

questions.prompt: Match each reconciliation exception from Lesson 15 to its correct handling.
left: Bank fees/interest with no system counterpart
Amount mismatch from an in-transit transfer fee
Amount mismatch from a data-entry transposition error
right: Leave unreconciled until the bank actually clears it — a normal timing difference, not an error
Correct the receipt amount in Receivables to match the actual wire, then reconcile
Create the missing external transaction so it has something to reconcile against, then reconcile
Record the deducted amount as a separate bank charge and reconcile the net
questions.explain: Bank fees need an external transaction created so they have something to reconcile against. Outstanding checks are left unreconciled until the bank clears them — that's expected, not broken. A fee deducted in transit gets recorded as a separate charge so the net reconciles. A transposed data-entry amount gets corrected in Receivables to the true figure.

questions.prompt: A customer says an invoice dated the 3rd of this month is missing from a statement run on the 1st of this month, which covers transactions dated through the last day of the prior month. What's the correct conclusion?
options: The invoice correctly falls outside this run's cutoff window; it isn't missing from Receivables and will appear on the next statement
The statement process is broken and needs to be rerun with different parameters
The invoice must have a hold preventing it from appearing on any statement
The customer's account must be excluded from this statement cycle entirely
questions.explain: A transaction can be entirely real and correctly entered and still not appear on a given statement run if it falls outside that run's date-range parameters — a timing exclusion, not a data or statement error. The resolution is explanation, not a data fix.

questions.prompt: In Oracle Fusion General Ledger, which period status allows journal entry but not posting?
options: Future Enterable
Open
Closed
Permanently Closed
Never Opened
Pending Close
questions.explain: Future Enterable (F) allows journal entry into the period but blocks posting. Open (O) allows full transaction activity, including posting, which is why it's the tempting wrong answer. Closed (C) and Permanently Closed (P) block new transactions, and Never Opened (N) blocks entry entirely.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B, Open, is the closest wrong answer because it also sounds permissive — but Open allows full transaction activity, posting included. Future Enterable is specifically the status where entry is allowed while posting itself is still blocked, which is the one detail that distinguishes the two.

questions.prompt: A 25-journal month-end batch fails to post. The posting log identifies one specific journal and line referencing a disabled account combination. The other 24 journals post successfully when run independently. What is the correct fix?
options: Correct only the one affected line to a current active account, leaving the other 24 journals untouched, then re-run posting for the batch
Re-enable the disabled account combination so the original line can post unchanged
Delete and recreate the entire 25-journal batch from scratch
Turn on suspense posting for the ledger so the unbalanced line posts automatically
questions.explain: One invalid line blocked the whole batch's posting attempt. Isolating whether it's one line or the whole batch turns a large emergency into a small correction — fix the one line to a current, confirmed account and leave the rest alone. Suspense posting is unrelated here, since the problem is a disabled account, not an unbalanced journal.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Journal Import error codes from Lesson 17.
options: EF04 means the account combination is invalid
EF03 means the account is disabled
EU02 means the entry is unbalanced, but suspense posting is allowed, so Oracle processes it anyway
WU01 is a warning rather than a failure, because suspense posting is allowed for that unbalanced entry
Turning on dynamic insertion is always the correct fix for an EF04 error
questions.explain: EF04 is invalid account, EF03 is disabled account, and WU01 is exactly the warning case — unbalanced, but suspense posting is allowed, so it processes anyway. EU02 is the opposite: unbalanced with suspense posting NOT allowed, which is a real failure. And turning on dynamic insertion isn't automatically correct — Lesson 17 specifically chose to create the account combination properly through Enterprise Structures instead, since dynamic insertion could create an incomplete or incorrectly structured combination for something like a cost center.

questions.prompt: Match each Subledger Accounting / GL transfer term to what it actually is.
right: Status confirming SLA has generated the journal entry and it's ready to transfer
A per-entry attribute that intentionally excludes an entry from any transfer run, regardless of how many times the program runs
The SLA program that generates a journal entry from a subledger transaction, in Draft or Final mode
The separate program that moves Final-mode journal entries into General Ledger as unposted journals
questions.explain: Create Accounting generates the journal entry. Transfer to GL is the separate program that moves a Final-mode entry into GL. Accounted – Final confirms the entry exists and is ready to transfer. A Transfer to GL indicator set to N intentionally excludes an entry from transfer, by design, no matter how many times the transfer program runs.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of diagnosing a period that won't close, per Lesson 20, in the correct order.
items: Open the Close Monitor / period close checklist for the ledger and period
Read which specific prerequisites are flagged as unmet
Recognize each blocker as a familiar ticket pattern, such as an unposted journal or an untransferred batch
Resolve each blocker using the method appropriate to its specific cause
Confirm the Close Monitor shows all prerequisites met, then close the period
questions.explain: A period-close ticket is rarely a new category of problem — the Close Monitor shows exactly which prerequisite is unmet, each blocker usually matches a pattern already diagnosed elsewhere (a stuck journal, a transfer gap), and once each is resolved specifically, the checklist confirms the period is actually ready to close.

questions.prompt: A company bought a new forklift in June. It's now August, and the forklift still shows no depreciation, while every other asset in the book depreciated normally for both months. Mass Additions shows the forklift's invoice line sitting On Hold with no asset category assigned. What is the most likely consequence once this is fixed?
options: Depreciation will need to catch up for June and July, not just start in August, because the in-service date is June
Depreciation will only start from August forward, since that's when the hold was cleared
The asset cannot depreciate at all until the next fiscal year begins
The missing asset category has no effect on depreciation timing, only on reporting
questions.explain: An asset still sitting in Mass Additions hasn't entered the active register yet, so it can't depreciate. Once posted, it should carry its actual in-service date (June here), meaning depreciation needs to catch up for the months it missed rather than simply starting from whenever it was finally posted.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Prepare Mass Additions derives the depreciation expense account by taking the invoice distribution's clearing account and overlaying its natural account segment with the natural account segment of the ________ defined on the asset category.
questions.explain: If the asset category assigned to a line has no depreciation expense account defined for the relevant book, there's nothing to overlay with, and the line goes On Hold — exactly the cause behind Lesson 22's six stuck delivery trucks.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about job roles, data roles, and security profiles, per Lesson 24.
options: A job role determines whether a user can see a page or function at all
A data role combines a job role with a specific data security grant
A security profile defines the actual scope, such as business unit or ledger, that a data role grants access to
A user who can open a page but sees zero data for one business unit always has a function-privilege problem, not a data-access problem
Segment value security and business-unit scoping from a data role's security profile are the exact same mechanism
questions.explain: Job role/function privilege controls whether the page or function is visible at all. A data role combines a job role with a data security grant, and a security profile is what actually defines its scope. Seeing the page but zero data for one BU is specifically a data-access problem, not a function-privilege one — and segment value security (Lesson 25) is a separate, finer-grained mechanism, distinct from business-unit scoping.

questions.prompt: Match each Mass Additions queue status to what it actually means.
right: Already converted into an active asset by Post Mass Additions
Freshly arrived from Payables, not yet processed by Prepare Mass Additions
Ready — set manually or defaulted once a line is confirmed good
Prepare Mass Additions ran but couldn't derive required information
questions.explain: New lines haven't been processed yet. On Hold lines failed derivation during Prepare Mass Additions. Post means the line is confirmed ready. Posted means Post Mass Additions already converted it into an active asset.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of diagnosing an expense report stuck "In Progress" with no pending approver, per Lesson 23, in the correct order.
items: Open BPM Worklist as an administrator and find the report's approval history
Read the routing history to confirm no pending task was ever assigned to anyone
Check the employee's HR record for a missing or incorrect manager assignment
Connect the missing manager to the rule logic that could not build an approver chain
Correct the HR record, then withdraw and resubmit the report
questions.explain: The evidence for an approval-routing problem lives in BPM Worklist, not in any accounting screen. Confirming no task was ever assigned narrows it to a routing failure, checking HR surfaces the missing manager, and connecting that gap to the rule logic explains why no approver chain could be built — which is why the actual fix lives in HR, not in Expenses.

questions.prompt: An analyst bulk-loads 150 AP invoice lines using an FBDI template, after deleting a column she wasn't using instead of leaving it blank. Load Interface File for Import fails immediately with zero rows loaded. What is the correct fix?
options: Re-create the data file from a fresh, unmodified copy of the template, leaving unused columns blank, then re-upload
Manually re-sequence the remaining columns in the file to account for the one that was deleted
Split the file into 150 separate single-row files and upload them one at a time
Switch from FBDI to ADFdi for this load, since FBDI doesn't support blank columns
questions.explain: Deleting a column breaks FBDI's fixed positional column structure and fails the load before any row is evaluated individually. The fix is file hygiene: start from a fresh, unmodified template and leave genuinely unused columns blank rather than removing them.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a REST API response with status code ________ means the request reached the server and was rejected for a content reason, such as a missing required field — not a credentials problem.
questions.explain: 400 Bad Request means the request reached the server and was rejected for a content reason. 401 Unauthorized, by contrast, means the request's credentials are missing, invalid, or expired — a completely different place to investigate.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about REST API errors and resource metadata, per Lesson 28.
options: A 401 Unauthorized points to authentication, such as token source or expiry, not the request body
A 400 Bad Request means the request never actually reached the server
A resource's describe metadata shows exactly which fields are actually required, distinct from the full schema
An Oracle quarterly update can change which fields are required on a REST resource with no change on the integration's own code
400 and 401 always point to the exact same root cause and are investigated the same way
questions.explain: 401 is an authentication problem; 400 means the request did reach the server and was rejected for a content reason, which is the opposite of never arriving. A resource's describe metadata narrows down exactly what's required, rather than guessing from the full schema. And a quarterly Oracle update can genuinely change required fields with zero change on the integration's side — which is exactly what happened in Lesson 28's ticket.

questions.prompt: Match each integration mechanism or response code to what it actually is.
right: A spreadsheet-based Excel add-in connecting directly to a Fusion page, suited to smaller, interactive data entry
The request's credentials are missing, invalid, or expired
A template-driven bulk load mechanism that stages data through an interface table before a separate import process
The request reached the server but was rejected for a content reason, like a missing required field
questions.explain: FBDI stages bulk data through an interface table ahead of a separate import step. ADFdi connects a spreadsheet directly to a page for smaller, interactive entry, with no staging table. 401 is a credentials problem. 400 is a content problem with a request that did reach the server.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of diagnosing a "the report shows the wrong numbers" ticket, per Lesson 29, in the correct order.
items: Get an exact, specific comparable number from the person reporting the discrepancy, not just "it's wrong"
Check when each number or report was actually generated
Determine what posted or changed in the gap between those two generation times
Re-run the report, or refresh the view, after confirming the relevant batch has posted
Explain to the reporter specifically why the two numbers differed, not just that they now match
questions.explain: "The report is wrong" is the vaguest possible ticket, so the first job is making it specific. From there, checking generation times and what changed in between reveals a timing difference rather than a data error, and the resolution isn't complete until the reporter understands why the numbers diverged in the first place, not just that they now agree.
